report:
Based on this research, I'd say the "false" characterization is too strong — the evidence is better described as preliminary/promising but inconclusive, not disproven.

## What the evidence actually shows

**Small positive trials exist.** Manber et al.'s 2010 RCT (Obstetrics & Gynecology, 150 pregnant women with MDD) found that women receiving a depression-specific acupuncture protocol had significantly greater symptom reduction and higher response rates than those receiving control acupuncture or massage (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/2010/03000/acupuncture_for_depression_during_pregnancy__a.7.aspx). A separate pilot RCT (described on academia.edu) reached similar preliminary conclusions (https://www.academia.edu/93899751/Preliminary_communication_Acupuncture_a_promising_treatment_for_depression_during_pregnancy).

**But independent, larger reviews are more cautious.** A rigorous Macquarie University RCT explicitly frames acupuncture as an "adjunct" needing further study, noting existing trials are few and results only "promising" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758005/). Cochrane's review of non-drug/non-psychological interventions for antenatal depression concluded that included trials (acupuncture among them) "were too small to reach any conclusions" and used inconsistent methods and outcomes, calling for further research (https://www.cochrane.org/th/evidence/CD006795_interventions-other-pharmacological-psychosocial-or-psychological-treating-antenatal-depression). NCCIH's broader summary of acupuncture evidence for depression is similarly guarded, noting sham-controlled trials for depressed mood give inconsistent results.

## Conclusion

The claim isn't clearly "false" — it's **unproven**. A few small, mostly single-group RCTs (notably Manber 2010) show statistically significant benefit versus control acupuncture, but sample sizes are small, blinding/sham-control design is difficult, and independent reviews (Cochrane, academic evaluations) say evidence is insufficient to draw firm conclusions. The accurate stance: acupuncture shows *preliminary, not confirmed* benefit for antenatal depression; more high-quality trials are needed before it can be endorsed as an evidence-based treatment.
